title: Divine Counsel and the Face of God
english: These are not creatures, but such states or dispositions. And teaching does the same: it takes the ignorant and makes him vanish, not as a man, but as an ignorant person; for it makes his ignorance vanish. In this way, righteousness makes the unrighteous vanish, not so that he no longer exists, but so that he no longer exists as unrighteous.

Lord, in your wrath confound them, and let fire devour them (Ps 53:3). Someone is confounded when he begins to waver and repent. And 'let fire devour them' means so that they no longer are such. 'You shall destroy their fruit from the earth and their seed from the sons of men' (Ps 53:10). The 'seed' is a homonym. When contrasted with fruit, it denotes the seed of a plant; but when contrasted with children, it is the seed of a man; for we have in the Scripture many times the 'seed' named after children. It is about the difference of the words that is now to be said.

This says: being upon the earth and having drawn near to the earth, they were stuck to it. Instead of the pure soul, the works of the flesh bore fruit. This is 'you shall destroy the fruit from the earth.' The earth is the good and beautiful thing, which, receiving the seed of Jesus that is cast, bears fruit. But the same earth, as a subject, is this one that bears thorns. And the receptive one is a rational substance of seeds. And from ourselves, this earth receives the difference.

'And their seed from the sons of men' (Ps 53:10). He sowed into the sons of men, not into the sons of God; for they are unfit for these. 'From the sons' therefore, 'of men you shall destroy their seed,' so that also the fitness toward the worthless fruit is lost. If someone has virtue by operation, the seed of wickedness is prevented, and the fitness and the power are [there], so that it seems to be destroyed.

'Because they turned to you for evil' (Ps 53:12), to you, having made them straight. Their choice turned toward the evil. You know that regarding sensible creations and idols, the one who has worked the evil work receives mockery, but the one who has done what is right receives praise. For it is said in Sirach: 'The work of a craftsman shall be praised' (Sir 38:33). ... if someone turns away from the 'according to the image.' How much then it reached to them, they judged evils toward you. 'They consulted plans' (Ps 53:12), which he would not be able...

To stand. And so that, having been led again by history from history—as if by a mere history, though I do not know if it is history—those who wished to build a tower, having the head up to the very limit, deliberated and were not able to stand. Indeed, they scattered. God perfects counsel when it is deliberated rightly and according to his will. He who pursues this 'does all things according to his counsel.' By this counsel, God brings a completion.

"You shall set them at their heels." It is often said of those concerning God that his body is [the church]; "you are the body of Christ," and in this body eyes, ears, and hands are found. Therefore, "you shall set" "them at their heels." You shall arrange these behind your body. This can be understood thus: the preceding things are called the face of God, and these created, sensible things are behind; for they are with him. Indeed, just as Moses at the end was not able to behold the face of God, God passes by with his glory and shows him the things behind. Indeed, he immediately wrote down the generation. Therefore, he shall set them at their heels; for the face is set toward the saints according to the prayer they offer up: "let your face shine upon us and we shall be saved." "In your remnants you will prepare your face." The remnants are the other saints besides those who "hate," those who were left over in the destruction. And it is well that it is "you will prepare" and not "you will give." It holds it ready so that everyone wishing to see it is able to see it.

"Be exalted, O Lord, in your power." We shall sing and indeed chant your mighty acts. For you do all these things powerfully. And after the beginning of the chanting, the power of God is praised: "Lord, the king shall rejoice in your power." The power that rejoices the king and performs all the things spoken of is exalted, not rising from a low place to a height, but no longer being thought of by men as lowly, but high as it is. And if we say, "I will exalt you, O Lord," we do not mean that we are lifting you up from the low to the height. To exalt is to confess him; that is the height. Therefore, he sings triumphantly—for power is spoken of a king alone, and of this king there are powers—things that can be done kingly. Toward the end, on behalf of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Psalm as the Voice of the Savior
english: The morning perception; a psalm of David. It is a spiritual day being made by the 'Sun of Righteousness,' about which much is laid down in the Scriptures, and especially in the New; 'as in a day,' he says, 'let us walk decently' (Ps 90:12). You know that even according to the literal sense, those doing something shameful do so in darkness, and especially then, when many good people were present. He who is, therefore, in ignorance of the existing good, is in darkness and does many things bringing shame. But when one is illumined by the light of the true one, 'walking in the day,' that is, progressing—for walking signifies progress—he does and thinks all things decently, nothing of those bringing shame.

The prophet Isaiah also presents this state, saying: 'My spirit cries out to you, O God, in the night' (Isa 26:9). This, therefore, is the morning perception; for even if we have illumination and the beginning of the day, we beg for the light to be present, so that the day may not fail, so that it may not be unable. 'Unto the end,' therefore, 'for the morning perception'; for having begun the day according to the perception of God, if the one perceiving remains in the same intention toward the one helping, he remains in that perception until the whole day; for if he perceives something in the beginning having only a little light, he perceives much more when it becomes midday. You find many such things lying in the Scriptures. God appeared to Abraham at no other time than at midday; for then the light had become at its peak. Moreover, the sun is at its zenith as if to be a shadowless thing to the air around us. But he says these things more allegorically, since even the literal sense leads to this.

This is also what the bride says to her own bridegroom: 'Tell me, whom my soul has loved, where do you graze and where do you gaze at midday?' (Song 3:1-4). At the beginning of the day, by which you graze, I have become. But I seek the midday time, when the light is at its peak. 'Where do you graze, where do you gaze?' so that being there as a companion with you, I may work the work; for I too want those sheep, which you graze, to graze. And the holy women who were shepherds, such as Rebekah, bring a symbol of such a state. 'For the' 'morning perception.' But who has the morning and the...

Is it possible to say at the beginning of the day, 'the night has passed, the day has approached'? For this reason also the women seeking Jesus, when he was crucified, did not see him at the midday hour (Matt 27:45), but from early morning. You know therefore also that the history concerning the Savior truly holds in general regarding everything significant, in which his works shine more than human things as light. We say that it happens in the morning time, when it takes hold of illumination so as to say: 'early I will stand before you and watch.' Such is also this: 'for you were darkness, but now in the light of the Lord' (Eph 5:8). 'Unto the end,' therefore, since the expected thing attained its end, which the economy of the Savior established and perfect virtue.

Listen then: this psalm is single-personed. That which says 'person' from the beginning until the end is the same. And there occur often in psalms and in prophecies shifts of persons, both of those speaking and toward what is being said and concerning what is being said; for everyone who speaks carries the person of the one announcing. And since he does not speak as it happens, but speaks to certain [people], there is also a second person: the one hearing the speaker and the matter concerning which he announces. The speaking [part] therefore is one person here.

And many things were taken from this psalm in the New Covenant, as if spoken from the person of the Savior, the one the psalm is said to be. Entirely this is so: 'the God, my God' (Ps 22:1); the Savior, encountering the cross, said this voice. And 'they divided my garments among themselves' (John 19:24) was also said by the Savior, having been said in the Gospels. And 'I will announce your name to my brothers' (Heb 2:26); Paul in the Hebrews wrote that this was said from the person of the Savior. Since, therefore, three testimonies lie here from the psalm, that the speaker is the person of the Savior, the whole psalm must be received as having been announced from his person.

And I say this necessarily—and I have also inserted it in those [works] concerning the Incarnation—since they always present to us words as if concerning the body of the Savior having existed, such as: 'but a body I have prepared for myself,' and: 'Christ suffering in the flesh for us,' we say that: if it were appropriate 'only': 'but only a body I have prepared for myself.' There is sometimes to wear more garments. If someone says concerning someone, 'look, I have a cloak, I have a tunic, a garment...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction between reality and the concept of error
english: Let him not add 'only', for he is not forbidden to have the others. Again, let one have, bring, a shield and a sword and a helmet and a breastplate. If it is necessary to say that I have a shield, let him not add 'only', for it is not denied that he has the others. We have here said by him concerning the person: 'Save my soul from the sword.' Even if in another place he says, 'I have prepared a body for me', and there was no memory of the soul, and here there is a memory of the soul, and not yet that he says, 'Save my soul from the sword', he has spoken concerning the soul of himself alone.

2 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1). The name of the forsaking, when spoken literally, does not reveal becoming being in darkness. For the martyrs, indeed, were not forsaken, though they were cast into the boiling pot. But those who sacrifice, even if they suffer nothing, were forsaken. When someone asks not to be forsaken, he asks this so as not to fall from his purpose. It seems that falling into abandonment does not happen to one suffering nothing, but sometimes it happens to him through malice, as I said, of the sacrificers. Abandonment, therefore, is the turning away of God from the one being forsaken.

Which Saul experienced: 'You have not listened to me,' he says, 'nor even in sleep' (1 Samuel 28:6); and he went toward the medium. If ever, therefore, you see a rich Christian having everything well, but having haste toward astrologers or toward necromancers or toward such things, these were forsaken. And if you see a poor man having fallen from wealth, but possessing God, such as Job was (Job 1:1), this one was not forsaken.

Since, therefore, the Savior came to a cross, and it seems to men to be abandonment to fall by such a death, he says this toward their assumption: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1). Perhaps he also speaks of abandonment as if of his own body; for the Hebrews were a body to him before this. Therefore, that people was forsaken. And he speaks of his own abandonment, since he was their head. 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1); he demands the cause and the end of the abandonment, for what it is. 'For what reason have you forsaken me?'; he is demanding an end, not so that it might be known to him, but so that [it might be known] to the body.
His, to his own men. Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions.

Here, so that we do not begin to mythologize, we are compelled to grasp a deeper theory. A thing and the concept of that thing are not the same. Many know the sensible things, but do not have a concept of them. It is a great thing to have a concept of realities. For in this way we separate a thing from the concept of the thing. And I mentioned color and appearance. But color is one thing and appearance is another, though they are inseparable from one another. Therefore, we separate them by concept. Color receives the more and the less. But appearance does not receive the more and the less, so that the color of the appearance is something different, even if it is never separated from it, even if it never exists without it. These things are said by those having a demonstration by subtraction. We subtract by concept this from that; it will not be sensed, it will not exist. When, therefore, we say that a line is a simple length, the sensible one is not simple. It certainly has width. But we subtract by concept.

I say: those who have transgressions that they will sense and that will exist do not know their concepts; for if they had known that it is harmful, that it turns toward destruction, they would not be acting them out. But there is having the concept of a transgression; for example, let it be a transgression being done against the law of God, such as to murder a man somehow. But when some judicial authority, serving the righteous law, puts to death the one worthy of death, just as Agag was murdered by Samuel (1 Sam 15:33), Elijah had the concept of a transgression, not a transgression, and Samuel. For the Savior says according to the man: for he himself is the one who has lost hope, the one saying these things: "Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions" (Ps 38:13). Not "are far from my salvation"; for he did not know sin, he did not do it. But I have it by concept; I know what sin is. And therefore the words of transgressions were far from my salvation. Let my salvation not take a mixture so as to be darkened. For sometimes someone is saved because of something inherent in him as good; if it is evil, his salvation is diminished. Many, indeed, have often asked: if someone does many evils, but does a few goods, does he perish? To say that he perishes is a subtraction of the hope of the persons.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
